arxiv-2404.01833.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have risen significantly in popularity and are increasingly being adopted across multiple applications. These LLMs are heavily aligned to resist engaging in illegal or unethical topics as a means to avoid contributing to responsible AI harms. However, a recent line of attacks, known as jailbreaks, seek to overcome this alignment. Intuitively, jailbreak attacks aim to narrow the gap between what the model can do and what it is willing to do.

arxiv-2404.01833.text: In this paper, we introduce a novel jailbreak attack called Crescendo. Unlike existing jailbreak methods, Crescendo is a simple multi-turn jailbreak that interacts with the model in a seemingly benign manner. It begins with a general prompt or question about the task at hand and then gradually escalates the dialogue by referencing the model's replies progressively leading to a successful jailbreak. We evaluate Crescendo on various public systems, including ChatGPT, Gemini Pro, Gemini-Ultra, LlaMA-2 70b and LlaMA-3 70b Chat, and Anthropic Chat.

arxiv-2508.00500.text: Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly operate across domains such as robotics, virtual assistants, and web automation. However, their stochastic decision-making introduces safety risks that are difficult to anticipate during execution. Existing runtime monitoring frameworks, such as AgentSpec, primarily rely on reactive safety rules that detect violations only when unsafe behavior is imminent or has already occurred, limiting their ability to handle long-horizon dependencies.

arxiv-2508.00500.text: We present ProbGuard, a proactive runtime monitoring framework for LLM agents that anticipates safety violations through probabilistic risk prediction. ProbGuard abstracts agent executions into symbolic states and learns a Discrete-Time Markov Chain (DTMC) from execution traces to model behavioral dynamics. At runtime, the monitor estimates the probability that execution will remain safe from the current state, and triggers an intervention when this probability falls below a user-defined threshold.

arxiv-2508.00500.heading: Evaluation & Key Findings
arxiv-2508.00500.text: To improve robustness, ProbGuard incorporates semantic validity constraints in the abstraction and admits a PAC-style analysis that characterizes the sample complexity required to certify the learned model under standard assumptions. We evaluate ProbGuard in two safety-critical domains: autonomous driving and embodied household agents. Across evaluated scenarios, ProbGuard consistently predicts traffic law violations and collisions in advance, with warnings up to 15.84 seconds at a threshold yielding no false alarms, and up to 38.66 seconds at stricter thresholds. In embodied agent tasks, ProbGuard's re-prompting intervention mode reduces unsafe behavior by 65.37% relative to the unmonitored baseline while retaining 80.4% of the baseline task completion; a stricter halting configuration reduces unsafe behavior by 93.60% at a larger cost in completion.

Through critical analysis of 18 defense mechanisms reported in prior work, we identify that most achieve less than 50\% mitigation against sophisticated adaptive attacks. note-2026-ai-security-trajectory-monitor.text: - Per-turn checks are structurally blind to gradual escalation. Every defense in this collection adds state: a score, a hidden state, a geometry, or a risk chain that persists across turns. - The evidence is early. Most results use small, synthetic, or template-generated data and no shared benchmark exists, so headline numbers (F1 0.84, recall 90.8%, ASR 0.2-4.0%) are not comparable across papers. - The endpoint is a separate problem. EDR sees a trusted agent process doing authorized work; the manipulation happens in what the agent reads and decides. Endpoint vendors and CSA argue this; the numbers behind it are vendor-authored. - Cross-session accumulation is the least-covered case. One survey reports no benchmark coverage for it.

research-formal-verification-languages-i.text: In chip and semiconductor design, Formal Verification Languages provide the mathematical foundation for specifying and proving Register-Transfer Level (RTL) and architectural invariants before silicon fabrication. The industrial backbone comprises IEEE 1800 SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) and IEEE 1850 Property Specification Language (PSL) for linear temporal logic (LTL) Formal Property Verification (FPV), complemented by multi-modal verification and hardware construction languages including UCLID5 (SMT-backed datapath/control modeling), Chisel/FIRRTL (ChiselFV), and Coq-embedded theorem-proving frameworks such as Kami.

research-sat-and-smt-solvers-application.text: Primary literature synthesized in this collection — MonoSAT: Modulo Theories for Graphs, Networks, and Geometry (arxiv-1402.4677); cvc5: A Versatile and Industrial-Strength SMT Solver (arxiv-2201.04663); A Survey of Symbolic Execution Techniques for Software Development and Verification (arxiv-1610.00502); SAT and SMT-Based Automated Reasoning for Description Logics and Formal Ontologies (arxiv-1507.01763) — spans three synergistic pillars: (1) **Software Development & Symbolic Execution** (KLEE, CBMC, Dafny, cvc5), where path constraints over bit-vectors and arrays synthesize bug-triggering inputs and prove memory-safety invariants; (2) **Graph Analysis Modulo Theories** (MonoSAT), where monotonic graph predicates (reachability, shortest path, maximum s-t flow, minimum spanning tree, and DAG acyclicity) are decided natively inside DPLL(T) without propositional blowup; and (3) **Ontology & Description Logic Reasoning** (OWL 2, EL/ALC, SHACL, OntoLogic), where TBox/ABox concept subsumption, consistency, and numerical datatype constraints reduce directly to Horn-SAT and SMT.
